new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is predictable (non-phonemic) and falls on the penultimate syllable. A word-final phonetically long vowel (historically from *-VR/*-Vy) counts as a single syllable and does not draw stress, so stress stays on the syllable before it (ˈʔikuː); a word-final sequence of two identical vowels (geminate/double vowel) counts as two syllables, so stress falls on the first of them (tuˈmuːʔ = tumuuʔ).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Authors note they sometimes marked secondary stress in their own wordlist transcriptions but state no rule for it.
new_statements.exceptions: Only the final long-vowel vs geminate-vowel distinction (stress placement is what distinguishes ˈCVCVː from CVˈCVV); differences in stress placement between wordlists from different transcribers are flagged as possible mistranscriptions (p.31, note i). No lexical exceptions listed.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns isolated citation forms elicited for 12 wordlists (all three Saluan dialects: Loinang, Luwuk, Kintom-Pagimana-Boalemo, plus closely related Batui); it is a transcription note in a dialect-survey report, not a full phonological analysis. Root-medial consonant lengthening after the stressed vowel noted for the Baloa' (Honbola) subdialect only (ˈmatːa 'eye').
new_statements.identity_note: Mead & Pasanda's statement is made for Saluan as a whole on the basis of wordlists from all three dialects they recognise (Loinang incl. Lingketeng/Baloa'/Kahumama'on subdialects, Luwuk, Kintom-Pagimana-Boalemo) and is applied equally to the closely related Batui lect (Glottolog batu1255), which they treat as a separate language; the former Ethnologue split 'Coastal Saluan' vs 'Kahumamahon Saluan' is merged by them into one language = salu1253. Karsana et al. 2012 describe the Pagimana/Luwuk varieties.

sources.note: Appendix B, B.1 transcription notes, (a) p.29: 'In general, stress is non-phonemic, occurring on the penultimate syllable'; (d) p.30: final long vowels 'do not attract stress, which falls on the preceding (viz. penultimate) syllable', geminate VV sequences behave as two syllables (ˈsiku 'elbow', ˈʔikuː 'tail', tuˈmuːʔ 'live'). Stress (incl. sometimes secondary stress) marked on all forms the authors elicited themselves across 12 Saluan/Batui sites. Sec. 3.1 gives duration measurements for final long vs regular vowels.
